ReferenceThis page is detail behind the Stage 1 guide. You can build without reading it: each step of the guide links to the section it needs when something goes wrong. Like everything in Tailwhip, it is designed and simulated, not built.

AI-generated, designed and simulated, not built. Nothing on this page has been wired, powered or measured. Every number is tagged [D] datasheet or seller listing, [E] estimate, [C] chosen by this design, or [S] from the stage 1 simulation (sim.py). The meter readings in the power-up checklist are gates: do not connect the next part until you get the reading the table gives.

This page covers the stage 1 balancer only: one dual-shaft TT motor, two 18650 cells, an ESP32, a GY-521 and an MX1508. It gives you the circuit, where every wire goes on the robot, the current each part draws, and the order to power it up in. Board positions, mounts and cable routes follow the final stage1.py and mechanical.md. The published Tailwhip's electronics page (docs/electronics.md) uses the same parts and the same reference numbers where a part is shared, so stage 1 carries into stage 2 without rewiring the power section.

Stage 1 is built in two milestones. Milestone A balances on the IMU alone: everything on this page except the section "Milestone B: wheel sensor". Milestone B adds one wheel sensor so the robot can hold its position. It plugs in without re-soldering anything on the robot. Every milestone B item is marked (B) in the tables and drawn dashed in both drawings.

Drawings:

  • schematic.svg: the full circuit, every pin of every board by the name printed on it.
  • wiring.svg: the robot itself, both faces of the mast unfolded, with every wire drawn end to end in the colour to use. You should be able to wire the robot from this drawing alone.
  • electronics.json: the same model in machine-readable form (parts, every pin, nets, wires, ESP32 pin map, power budget).

All three come from tools/gen_electronics.py. It checks that every net is joined end to end by a wire or an on-board connection (nothing implied), that every pin of every board is drawn, that the pin numbers and constants in ../firmware/stage1_balance/stage1_balance.ino match the circuit, and that no labels overlap.

How it works (block diagram in words)

2 x 18650 (BT1, unprotected) -- B+ / BM / B- --> 2S BMS (U3)
U3 P+ --> F1 PTC 3 A --> SW1 power switch --> K2 plug --> JB --> VBAT_SW, 6.0-8.4 V
                     \--> J1 charge jack (also on U3 P-), before the switch
VBAT_SW --> U4 MX1508 + pad (470 uF C1 across + / -) --> MOTOR-A --> K1 plug --> M1 TT motor (100 nF C3 across the tabs)
        --> U1 Mini360 (5.0 V) --> U5 ESP32 5V pin --> DevKit regulator --> 3V3 --> U6 GY-521
        --> R1 100k / R2 33k divider on JB --> VSENSE --> ESP32 GPIO36
ESP32 GPIO25, GPIO26 --> MX1508 IN1, IN2 (100k pull-downs R3, R4)
ESP32 GPIO21 (SDA), GPIO22 (SCL) <--> GY-521 SDA, SCL (pull-ups on the GY-521)
GND = BMS P-. Everything else's ground returns there.

The cells have no protection of their own, so the first thing their current meets is the BMS. It disconnects the pack on over-discharge (about 2.5 V per cell), over-charge, over-current and short circuit, and it balances the two cells near full charge. From the BMS output the current goes through the PTC fuse and the power switch to the K2 plug and into the junction board, which is the robot's battery rail (VBAT_SW) and its star ground.

The MX1508 takes VBAT_SW directly. The ESP32 drives its IN1 and IN2 with 20 kHz PWM in slow-decay mode; its MOTOR-A outputs drive the TT motor through the K1 plug. The Mini360 buck makes 5.0 V from VBAT_SW for the ESP32's 5V pin; the DevKit's own regulator makes 3.3 V from that, and the GY-521 runs from the ESP32's 3V3 pin. A 100k / 33k divider scales the battery to 0.248 of its voltage for the ESP32's ADC on GPIO36, so the firmware can cap the motor voltage at 6.0 V and stop at a low battery.

Battery safety and charging

Read this before you put cells in the holder. It is the same as the published robot, because the pack is the same.

  • The cells are unprotected. Nothing inside them stops an over-discharge, an over-charge or a short. The BMS does that job, so it is wired before anything else and nothing ever connects to the cells except through it. Never connect anything to B- other than the cell: everything else's ground is P-.
  • Genuine high-drain cells, a matched pair: same model and age, within 0.05 V of each other before they go in (Molicel P28A, Samsung 25R or 30Q, Sony VTC6). Never "UltraFire", "GTF" or "9900 mAh" cells.
  • Check each cell first: 3.0 to 4.2 V on the meter. Retire a cell under 2.5 V, dented, with a torn wrap, or warm at rest.
  • Wire the BMS in this order: B- first, then BM, then B+. Undo it in reverse. Many 2S boards read 0 V on P+ / P- until a charger has been connected once.
  • Charge with SW1 off, through J1, with an 8.4 V CC/CV Li-ion charger at about 1 A, on a non-flammable surface, attended. The pack is about 2.5-3 Ah, so a charge from empty takes about 3 h [E]. The BMS stops the charge if a cell goes over about 4.25-4.3 V [E listings] and bleeds the higher cell near full [D listing]. Once a month, measure both cells at full charge: more than 0.05 V apart, charge each one alone in a single-cell smart charger.
  • J1 accepts any 5.5 x 2.1 mm plug, including 9 V and 12 V wall adapters. Label it "8.4 V Li-ion only". Check the charger's plug is centre positive with the meter before first use.
  • Switch off after every run. The firmware stops driving the motor at 6.4 V (3.2 V per cell), but the ESP32 and the buck keep drawing about 50 mA [E] until the BMS cuts off at about 2.5 V per cell. The cells survive that, but it is a deep discharge.
  • No reverse-polarity protection except what the Pololu switch has. Check the holder's polarity with the meter at power-up step 2, before any board is connected.

At the battery

In slow decay the battery supplies the motor only during the drive part of each PWM cycle, so battery current is about duty x motor current, and part of the time the motor returns current to the pack.

Case Logic (pack side) Motor (pack side) Pack current
Switched on, waiting (not armed) 0.05 A 0 ≈ 0.06 A [E]
Balancing on a flat floor 0.05 A 0.09-0.13 A mean [S] ≈ 0.15-0.2 A [S+E]
Recovering from a shove 0.06 A up to 1.0-1.34 A [S] ≈ 1.4 A for a moment [S+E]
Motor stalled at the 6.0 V cap (held, wheel blocked) 0.06 A 1.5 A x duty 0.71-0.94 ≈ 1.1-1.5 A [D+E]
Worst second: full-speed reversal 0.06 A up to about 2-3 A ≈ 3 A for tens of ms [E]

A pair of 2500-3000 mAh cells (about 2.5 Ah usable [E]) runs this for many hours of balancing. Charge, not run time, is the limit you will hit.

Voltage sag

Two good cells (15-20 mΩ each [E]), the BMS MOSFETs (about 10 mΩ [E]), the fuse (50-100 mΩ [E]), the switch, K2 and 22 AWG leads come to roughly 0.15-0.2 Ω. That is 0.03 V at 0.2 A and 0.3 V at 1.5 A. The firmware reads the battery 10 times a second and sets duty = u x 6.0 V / VBAT, so a sag does not change what u = 1 means until VBAT is below 6.0 V.

Protection chain: cells → BMS → PTC → switch → rail

Part Protects against Why it is needed even with the others
U3 BMS Over-discharge (about 2.5 V per cell), over-charge (about 4.25-4.3 V), over-current, short circuit; balances the cells The cells are unprotected. Without it, a stuck motor or a forgotten switch drains a cell to 0 V and a short has nothing to stop it.
F1 PTC 3 A A sustained overload or a short in the wiring after the BMS The BMS's short-circuit trip is set high (tens of amps [E]) to suit 10 A loads; a partial short of a few amps (a pinched wire, a damaged MX1508) is under it and would cook 26 AWG wire. The PTC trips at 6 A in seconds and resets when it cools.
SW1 Leaving it on It is the only way to turn the robot off without unplugging. It must carry all the motor current: 3 A rated, not a 0.3 A slide switch. The Pololu 2810 also has reverse-voltage protection [D Pololu].
K2 plug Mistakes during power-up and repairs Unplug it and every board is off the battery while the BMS, fuse and switch stay testable.

The charge jack J1 sits on the BMS output, before the fuse and the switch, so the charge current passes the BMS (which stops an over-charge) and not the switch.

Mini360: setting it to 5.0 V

There is no manufacturer datasheet for "Mini360": it is an MP2307-type synchronous buck on a 17 x 11 mm board, input 4.75-23 V, about 340 kHz, output set by a tiny pot [D listings]. It ships set to a random voltage, often 10 V or more, which kills an ESP32 at once.

  1. Wire it as the wiring list says (W13, W14 to the MX1508 pads; W15, W16 jumper halves on OUT+ and OUT-), but do not push W15 and W16 onto the ESP32 yet.
  2. Plug K2, switch on. Meter on DC volts across the two loose Dupont ends of W15 (red, +) and W16 (black, -).
  3. Turn the pot a little at a time with a small screwdriver, giving the meter a second to settle, until it reads 5.00 ± 0.05 V. On most boards clockwise lowers the voltage [E]; if it does not move, try the other way.
  4. Switch off and on again and check it still reads 5.00 V. Put a dab of nail varnish on the pot. Write "5V" on the board.
  5. Only then push W15 and W16 onto the ESP32's 5V and GND pins.

Below about 6 V in, the Mini360 cannot hold 5.0 V out and its output follows the input down [E]; the ESP32 keeps working to about 4.5 V on its 5V pin (the DevKit's AMS1117 needs about 1.1 V of headroom [D]). The firmware stops the motor at 6.4 V, well above that.

Battery sense: divider maths and ADC range

R1 100 kΩ from VBAT_SW to VSENSE, R2 33 kΩ from VSENSE to GND, C2 100 nF across R2. VSENSE goes to GPIO36 (SVP).

VSENSE = VBAT x 33 / (100 + 33) = 0.248 x VBAT. The firmware multiplies back by 133 / 33 = 4.03 (BATT_DIV).

Pack VSENSE (GPIO36) Meaning
8.4 V 2.08 V Full
7.4 V 1.84 V Nominal
6.4 V 1.59 V Firmware low-battery stop (LOW_BATT_MV 6400, for 2 s)
6.0 V 1.49 V Below this u = 1 can no longer reach 6.0 V
5.0 V 1.24 V BMS cut-off (about 2.5 V per cell)
  • ADC range check. The firmware sets 11 dB attenuation on GPIO36. Espressif gives the usable range at 11 dB as 150-2450 mV [D ESP-IDF ADC docs, ESP32]. The full pack gives 2.08 V, inside it with 0.37 V to spare; the highest pack voltage the ADC could read is 2.45 x 4.03 = 9.9 V, above anything a 2S pack can reach.
  • Accuracy. analogReadMilliVolts() uses the chip's factory calibration; expect within about ±2-3 % [E], plus 1 % from each resistor, so the reading is within about ±0.2 V at 8 V [E]. Compare it with the meter at power-up step 6.
  • Source impedance and C2. The divider looks like 100k ∥ 33k = 24.8 kΩ to the ADC. That is too high for the ADC's sampling capacitor to charge fully in one sample [E]; C2 holds the voltage steady and supplies the sample. The divider and C2 form a 2.5 ms low-pass, far faster than the firmware's 10 Hz reading and its own smoothing.
  • Drain. 63 µA at 8.4 V, and only with SW1 on: the divider is on the switched side.
  • Why GPIO36: an ADC1 channel (ADC2 does not work with the radio on, which matters in stage 2), input only, no internal pull resistors to upset the divider.
  • If the divider fails: with R2 open, GPIO36 reads high, the firmware thinks the pack is fuller than it is and drives a lower duty: the motor gets less than 6 V, not more. With the W17 jumper off, GPIO36 floats and the reading means nothing. If R1 is open, VSENSE reads 0 and the firmware assumes 7.4 V; on a full pack the motor then gets up to 6.8 V average for that run. Check the reading at step 6.

MX1508

Item Value
Supply 2-9.6 V [D datasheet via the BOM]; listings say 2-10 V. A full 2S pack is 8.4 V, 1.2 V under the limit. The motor supply is also the chip's supply; there is no separate logic pin.
Current One channel 1.5 A continuous / 2 A peak, the other 0.8 A / 1.5 A [D datasheet via the BOM]. Modules do not say which is which.
Control Two inputs per motor, no enable pin. IN1/IN2 high/low = forward, low/high = reverse, high/high = brake (motor shorted), low/low = coast (bridge off).
Inputs Driven at 3.3 V by the ESP32 (works on common modules [E]). R3, R4 100 kΩ pull them low when the ESP32 is not driving them.
PWM 20 kHz, 10-bit, from the ESP32's LEDC [C]. 80 MHz / 20 kHz = 4000 counts per period, so up to 11 bits would fit [D ESP32 LEDC]; 10 bits gives 1024 steps, about 8 mV each at the motor on a full pack. 20 kHz is above hearing.
Decay Slow decay [C]: one input held high, the other PWM-ed with the duty inverted. In the off-time the motor is shorted through the bridge, so the average motor voltage is duty x VBAT at any speed or load. That is the motor model the simulator uses. u = 0 brakes, exactly as the simulator's 0 V does. coast() (both low) is used when it is waiting or has fallen, so a falling robot does not have its wheels locked.
Voltage cap V_MOTOR_MAX = 6.0 V [C]: duty = u x 6.0 / VBAT, so u = 1 is 6.0 V average whatever the charge. On a full pack the largest duty is 6.0 / 8.4 = 0.71; at the 6.4 V low-battery stop it is 0.94. The TT motor is rated 3-6 V [D]. The peak voltage across the motor in each PWM pulse is still the full pack voltage; that is normal for a PWM-driven brushed motor and the 6 V rating is about average voltage (heat and brush wear).
Bench command motor <u> <ms> goes through the same drive(), so it is capped at 6.0 V too.

If channel A is the weak one. Symptoms: the robot balances, then cuts out or gets weak after a few seconds of hard work, and one side of the MX1508 is hot to the touch. Move W18 and W19 to IN3 and IN4, and W20 and W21 to MOTOR-B, and move R3 and R4 to IN3 and IN4. No firmware change. If both channels struggle, a DRV8833 module (1.5 A RMS, 2 A peak per channel [D TI]) or a TB6612FNG module (1.2 A continuous, 3.2 A peak per channel [D Toshiba]) uses the same two-input control; the TB6612 also needs its STBY pin tied high.

IMU wiring

The GY-521 sits 2 mm off the front face of the core, close to the axle, on two M2.5 self-tappers. Its cable is four 20 cm Dupont female-female jumpers: up the front of the core (tied at the core's two front tunnels, z 48 and 63), under the mast plate to the robot-right side at z 69, up outside the robot-right flanges, and round the flange's edge at z 98 to the back. W24 lands on the ESP32's lower header row; W25-W27 carry on up beside the antenna end of the board to the upper row. The other four GY-521 pins are not connected.

GY-521 pin (printed) Goes to ESP32 DevKit pin (printed) Wire Colour Where that ESP32 pin is
VCC 3V3 W24 red Row A (the row with 3V3 ... 5V), the pin at the antenna end: 19th from the USB end
GND GND W25 black Row B (the row with GND ... CLK), the pin at the antenna end: 19th from the USB end
SCL IO22 (D22, GPIO22) W26 yellow Row B, 3rd from the antenna end: 17th from the USB end
SDA IO21 (D21, GPIO21) W27 blue Row B, 6th from the antenna end: 14th from the USB end
XDA not connected Auxiliary I2C master for an external magnetometer. Unused.
XCL not connected Same.
AD0 not connected Pulled low on the GY-521 [E], so the address is 0x68, which the firmware expects (MPU = 0x68). Tied to 3V3 it would be 0x69 and the firmware would not find the sensor.
INT not connected Interrupt output. The firmware polls the sensor at 400 Hz instead.
  • Supply. VCC to the ESP32's 3V3, not 5V. The GY-521's own regulator then drops it to about 3.1-3.2 V [E], inside the MPU-6050's 2.375-3.46 V [D]. Its SCL and SDA pull-ups go to that regulated rail, so the bus idles at about 3.2 V, above the ESP32's 2.5 V logic-high threshold [D] and never above 3.3 V.
  • Pull-ups. Already on the GY-521 (2.2-4.7 kΩ depending on the board [E]). Add none. The ESP32's weak internal pull-ups are switched on by Wire as well; they do no harm.
  • Speed. 400 kHz (Wire.begin(21, 22, 400000)). With about 20 cm of jumper the bus is around 50 pF [E]; with a 4.7 kΩ pull-up the rise time is about 0.85 x 4.7 kΩ x 50 pF = 0.2 µs, inside the 0.3 µs fast-mode limit [D I2C spec]. Twist SCL and SDA loosely together with GND, and keep them away from the motor leads (the motor leads are on the back, the I2C wires on the front).
  • Mounting. Chip facing forward (away from the core), the silkscreen X arrow pointing up (readImu() maps body x = chip z, body y = -chip y, body z = chip x). Solder the header with its pins on the chip side, pointing forward, so the board lies flat on its posts. Check the X arrow before you screw it down: if it runs across the header, mount the board 21 mm wide and 16 mm tall, header along the top (as drawn); if it runs along the header, mount it 16 wide and 21 tall with the header on one side. The printed mount has pilots for both (mechanical.md, GY-521 orientation). Only if you must mount it some other way, change the six mapping lines in readImu().
  • Confirm it works (power-up step 6): 1. Flash firmware/i2c_scan (in the published robot's folder; same pins, 21 and 22). It must print SDA=1 SCL=1 and find 0x68 (WHO_AM_I 0x68, or 0x70 for an MPU-6500 clone, which also works). 2. Flash stage1_balance. The banner must not say MPU-6050 not found. Type show: with the robot upright, pitch reads near 0 deg. 3. Tilt the robot forward: pitch must go positive. Tilt it back: negative. If the sign is wrong, the board is mounted differently from the drawing.

ESP32 pin map

The board is an ESP32 DevKitC, 38 pins (Espressif's layout). Its two header rows are called row A (3V3, EN, SVP ... 5V, Espressif's J1) and row B (GND, IO23, IO22 ... CLK, J3). On the robot it lies across the back of the mast with the module facing the mast, USB toward the robot's left, on four corner pads with two zip ties between the header rows, so the pins point back at you and the printed labels are on the far side. Count pins from the USB end. Row A is the lower row.

GPIO Printed label Row, pin from USB end Net Dir Use Checks
25 IO25 (D25) A, 11 M_IN1 out MX1508 IN1, LEDC PWM 20 kHz Not a strapping pin. Floats at reset: R3 pull-down.
26 IO26 (D26) A, 10 M_IN2 out MX1508 IN2 Not a strapping pin. Floats at reset: R4 pull-down.
21 IO21 (D21) B, 14 SDA i/o GY-521 SDA Fine.
22 IO22 (D22) B, 17 SCL out GY-521 SCL Fine.
36 SVP (VP) A, 17 VSENSE in Battery divider, ADC1_CH0, 11 dB Input only, no internal pulls: right for an ADC.
2 IO2 (D2) B, 15 LED out On-board LED, no wire Strapping pin: must be low or open to enter download mode; the LED and its resistor hold it low. Fine.
34 IO34 (D34) A, 15 IR_D0 in (B) Wheel sensor D0 (W30) Input only, no internal pulls: R5 100k pull-down and C4 10 nF at K3. Not a strapping pin. Open in milestone A (the firmware detects a floating input).
- 5V (VIN) A, 1 5V pwr From Mini360 OUT+ (W15) See "USB and the battery together".
- GND A, 6 GND pwr To Mini360 OUT- (W16); (B) also the wheel sensor through the Y-lead W29
- 3V3 A, 19 3V3 pwr To GY-521 VCC (W24); (B) also the wheel sensor through the Y-lead W28 The DevKit regulator's output: about 10 mA used, 30 mA with the sensor.
- GND B, 19 GND pwr To GY-521 GND (W25)

Avoided, and why: GPIO0, 5, 12 and 15 are strapping pins (GPIO12 in particular sets the flash voltage at reset and must stay low); GPIO6-11 (SD0-SD3, CMD, CLK) are the flash; GPIO1 and 3 are the USB serial; GPIO34, 35 and 39 are input only. None of them is used, except GPIO34 for the milestone B wheel sensor (input only is right for it). Every unused pin is left open.

30-pin DevKit instead? Same GPIOs, different positions: wire by the printed label (D25, D26, D21, D22, VP, VIN, 3V3, GND), not by position. On the common 30-pin DOIT board, VP, D25, D26 and VIN are on one row and D21, D22, GND and 3V3 on the other.

USB and the battery together. You need both while tuning (the motor runs from the battery, the serial monitor from USB). Espressif's DevKitC guide says to use only one power source at a time; many DevKit boards have a diode between the USB 5 V and the 5V pin that makes both together safe, some do not [D Espressif DevKitC guide; E clones]. Check yours at power-up step 0: with USB only, measure the 5V pin to GND. About 4.6-4.8 V means there is a diode; 5.0 V means there is none, and you must not plug USB in while SW1 is on (use a USB cable with the 5 V wire cut, or a USB isolator).

USB alone, switch off. With USB plugged in and SW1 off, the ESP32's 5 V rail can feed backwards through the Mini360 into the battery rail and the MX1508, which may sit at about 4-4.7 V [E]. The firmware then sees a low battery after 2 s and will not balance, which is safe, but the bench command motor does not check the battery and would draw the motor current from your laptop's USB port. Do not run motor without SW1 on.

Decoupling

Part Where Why
C1 470 µF 16 V low-ESR Legs on the MX1508 + and - pads, stripe to - Supplies the motor's 20 kHz pulse current locally so the pack leads do not have to, and catches the motor's inductive kick when the bridge switches. Ripple: at 1.5 A and duty 0.71 the capacitor carries about 1.5 x √(0.71 x 0.29) = 0.7 A RMS [E] for a moment, and about 0.2 A RMS while balancing; a 470 µF 16 V low-ESR part handles that [E]. Voltage ripple about 1.5 A x 0.29 x 50 µs / 470 µF = 0.05 V.
C2 100 nF Across R2 on JB Holds VSENSE steady for the ADC (see "Battery sense").
C3 100 nF ceramic Across the motor tabs, legs short, in the 5 mm pocket above the can Brush noise at the source [D Pololu]. It adds a small charging spike on each PWM edge (about 0.8 µC at 8.4 V), harmless for the MX1508. If you see the MX1508 warm at standstill, try 10 nF.
On-board Mini360, ESP32 DevKit, GY-521 Each has its own input and output capacitors [E]. Nothing extra is needed.
If the ESP32 resets when the motor starts 100 µF across the ESP32's 5V and GND pins Not in the design. Add it only if step 7 shows resets (rst: lines in the serial monitor).

Grounds

One star point: JB GND, fed from BMS P- through K2 (W8). From there:

  • W12 (22 AWG) to the MX1508's - pad: all motor return current.
  • The Mini360's IN- comes off the MX1508's - pad (W14, 26 AWG); its OUT- is the same copper; W16 takes it to the ESP32. No motor current flows through the ESP32 or the I2C ground.
  • The GY-521's ground comes from the ESP32's other GND pin (W25).
  • R2 and C2 go to JB GND on the perfboard.
  • SW1 GND (W6) goes straight to BMS P-: the Pololu switch needs it to turn its MOSFET on.

Build the junction board

A piece of perfboard 8 holes wide by 5 tall, cut to about 21 x 13 mm to fit the rails. Top = up the robot.

  1. Solder the 2-pin XH header (K2) near the top edge, standing so the mated plug points forward: pin 1 (+) toward the middle of the robot, pin 2 (-) toward the edge.
  2. A VB bus row from K2 pin 1 down the left side, a GND bus row from K2 pin 2 along the bottom.
  3. R1 100k from VB to a VS pad; R2 33k from VS to GND; C2 100 nF beside R2, VS to GND.
  4. One male header pin on VS, pointing out, for the W17 jumper.
  5. Solder pads on VB and GND for W11 and W12.

Check with the meter before it goes on the robot: VB to GND about 133 kΩ; VS to GND about 33 kΩ (it rises for a moment while C2 charges); VB to VS about 100 kΩ; VB to GND never under 100 kΩ.

Power-up checklist

Each step has the reading to expect. Do not go on until you get it. Meter on DC volts unless the step says otherwise. Motor unplugged at K1 until step 7.

# Connect Do Expect
0 ESP32 alone on USB. Nothing else. Measure its 5V pin to GND and its 3V3 pin to GND. Flash stage1_balance, open the serial monitor at 115200. 5V pin: 4.6-4.8 V (diode on the board) or 5.0 V (no diode: see "USB and the battery together") [E]. 3V3: 3.30 ± 0.1 V. Serial: MPU-6050 not found .... The LED blinks fast (5 Hz).
1 Each cell, out of the holder Measure it 3.0-4.2 V each, within 0.05 V of each other.
2 Cells in the holder; BMS wired B-, BM, B+ (W2, W3, W1). Nothing on P+ / P-. Measure B+ to B-, BM to B-, then P+ to P-. B+ to B- = the sum of the two cells. BM to B- = the cell at the B- end. P+ to P- = the sum, or 0 V until a charger has been plugged in once (plug it in for a second). Red probe on the side you think is +: the reading must be positive.
3 F1, SW1 (W4, W5, W6), J1 (W9, W10), K2 housing (W7, W8). K2 not plugged in. SW1 off, then on. Measure across the K2 housing (pin 1 to pin 2) and across J1 (centre to sleeve). SW1 off: 0 V at K2. On: the pack voltage at K2, positive on pin 1. J1: the pack voltage, centre positive, with SW1 on or off. Switch off.
4 JB built and checked (see "Build the junction board"). JB on the robot with W11, W12; MX1508 with C1, R3, R4; Mini360 with W13, W14, W15, W16. W15, W16, W17, W18, W19 not on the ESP32. Ohm check first, K2 unplugged. Meter on ohms, JB side of K2: pin 1 to pin 2. Climbs as C1 charges, then settles in the kΩ range or higher. Under 100 Ω: a short. Stop.
5 Plug K2. SW1 on. Measure: MX1508 + to -; JB VS to GND; MX1508 MOTOR-A pad to pad; the loose W15 to W16 Dupont ends. Then set the Mini360 (see "Mini360: setting it to 5.0 V"). MX1508: pack voltage. VS: 0.248 x pack (2.08 V at 8.4 V, 1.84 V at 7.4 V). MOTOR-A: 0 V (R3, R4 hold IN1, IN2 low). W15 to W16: random until set, then 5.00 ± 0.05 V. Pack current, meter in series at K2 (10 A range): under 20 mA [E]. Switch off.
6 Push W15, W16 onto the ESP32 (5V, GND), W17 (SVP), W18 (IO25), W19 (IO26); then the GY-521 (W24-W27). USB unplugged. Hold the robot upright and still, SW1 on. Measure the ESP32's 5V and 3V3 pins. Then plug USB in (only if step 0 found a diode) and type show. Flash firmware/i2c_scan once if anything looks wrong. 5V: 5.0 V. 3V3: 3.30 ± 0.1 V. After about 1 s of gyro calibration the LED blinks at 2 Hz (waiting), and goes solid once it arms (held within 5 deg for 0.5 s; the motor is unplugged, so nothing moves). show: vbat within 0.2 V of your meter on the pack; pitch near 0 deg upright; tilt forward: pitch positive. i2c_scan: SDA=1 SCL=1, 0x68. Pack current about 0.06 A [E].
7 SW1 off. Plug K1 (motor plug, on the back of the core). Robot on a stand, wheels off the ground. SW1 on, USB in. motor 0.3 1000, then motor -0.3 1000. Meter across the MOTOR-A pads during a motor 0.5 3000. The wheels turn for 1 s each way, the top of the tyre moving forward for +0.3 (else dir -1, save). Meter: about 0.5 x 6.0 = 3 V average [E] (a meter shows the average of the PWM roughly). No reset messages in the serial monitor.
8 Meter in series at K2 (10 A range), robot on the stand. Idle, then motor 1 3000. Idle about 0.06 A [E]; no-load full speed about 0.2 A [E: 0.16 A x duty + logic]. Write both down, with the no-load wheel speed from the README's bench step 3.

Then carry on with the README's bring-up (gains, trim, stream 1). For milestone B, continue with steps B0-B4 in "Milestone B: wheel sensor".

Milestone B: wheel sensor

Milestone A builders: skip this whole section. Milestone A balances on the IMU alone, and everything above this section is a complete build without it. Milestone B adds one wheel sensor so the robot can hold its position. In both drawings the milestone B parts sit inside a dashed outline, and their wires are dashed.

What it is

The sensor is a TCRT5000 reflective IR sensor with its LM393 comparator module, the part the published Tailwhip uses. It reads a printed ring on the inside of the left wheel. The ring is 0.6 mm matte black PLA with 16 sector windows that show the wheel's yellow rim (mechanical.md). The firmware counts both edges of every window: 32 edges per turn, 11.25 deg or 6.4 mm of travel each.

The only place the ring can be seen is under the core, and the module (32 x 14 mm) does not fit there. So the mechanical design splits it in two:

  • U8, the bare TCRT5000, is desoldered from the module and pushed into a clip printed under core_left, at (x 0, y 6.4, z -20.5) mm. Its lenses face the ring 2.5 mm away.
  • U7, the module board (comparator, trimmer, LEDs), sits on rails on the back of the core (y -7..7, z 14..46), trimmer and LEDs facing back.
  • A 60 mm four-wire pigtail (W34-W37) joins U8's four legs to U7's four sensor pads.
  • The module's three-wire cable (VCC, GND, D0) goes through the K3 plug, just above the module. It then runs up the back of the core (tied with K1 at z 67.5), behind the MX1508, to the ESP32's row A.

The firmware (PIN_IR = 34, present in the sketch) counts edges on an interrupt with a 1 ms lockout. It trusts the sensor after 8 believable edges, and falls back to milestone A by itself if the sensor goes quiet or is noisy.

Connection From To Wire
3V3 ESP32 3V3 (row A, 19th pin from the USB end), Y-lead shared with the IMU's W24 K3 pin 1, then module VCC W28, W31
GND ESP32 GND (row A, 6th pin from the USB end), Y-lead shared with W16 K3 pin 2, then module GND W29, W32
D0 ESP32 IO34 (D34, GPIO34; row A, 15th pin from the USB end) K3 pin 3, then module D0 (printed DO on some boards) W30, W33
A0 (AO) not connected
IR LED anode module sensor pad A U8 leg A W34 (red)
IR LED cathode module sensor pad K U8 leg K W35 (black)
Detector collector module sensor pad C U8 leg C W36 (white)
Detector emitter module sensor pad E U8 leg E W37 (blue)

Which leg goes to which pad

The TCRT5000 has an IR LED (anode A, cathode K) and a phototransistor (collector C, emitter E) side by side. Vishay numbers the legs C, E, A, K [D Vishay TCRT5000]. On the common module the LED side is the one with the clear or blue lens, and the detector has the black lens [E]. Don't go by the lens colour or the silkscreen. Identify both ends with the meter before you cut anything:

  1. The module pads, module unpowered and the sensor still on it. Diode test from the module's GND pin: the pads that beep to GND are K and E. Of the other two, the one with a few hundred ohms to the VCC pin is A (the LED resistor). The one with about 10 kΩ to VCC is C (the detector pull-up) [E typical module]. Mark each pad with a fine pen, on the board, before anything moves.
  2. The sensor's legs, after it is off the board. Diode test across each pair. The LED pair reads about 1.1-1.2 V one way (red probe on A) and open the other way. The detector pair reads open both ways in the dark. Under a phone torch or daylight it may read a little one way: the red probe on that reading is C [E]. Mark the legs.
  3. Join A to A, K to K, C to C, E to E.

What a wrong pair does. At 3.3 V nothing is damaged: the TCRT5000's reverse limits are 5 V for both the LED and the detector [D Vishay]. A reversed LED stays dark. A reversed or swapped detector reads nothing. The module then never switches, and its D0 LED stays one way whatever is in front of the sensor. Swapped the other way round (LED where the detector goes), the LED gets only the 10 kΩ pull-up current and stays dark. So a wrong pair costs you a re-solder, not a part. The exception is 5 V: never power the module from 5 V during this test.

Taking the sensor off and extending it without cooking it

  • Cut, don't desolder, if you can. Snip the four legs close to the module board, leaving the sensor's legs as long as possible. Then clean the four pads with solder wick, or solder the pigtail to the leg stubs left in the board. The sensor never sees the iron for long. If you desolder instead, use a pump or wick, 330-350 °C [E], under 3 seconds a joint, and let it cool between joints.
  • Joints on the legs. Solder each pigtail wire at least 2 mm from the body (Vishay's limit is 260 °C for 10 s at 2 mm or more [D]). Hold the leg with tweezers between the joint and the body as a heat sink. Tin wire and leg first, then join them in one touch of about 1 s.
  • Leg length. The clip's lead slot lets the legs stick out about 2.5 mm behind the body (stage1.py). Cut each leg to about 4 mm, stagger the four joints along the wires so they cannot touch, and put 1.5 mm heat-shrink over each. Don't bend a leg at the body.
  • The wire. Four-core, 28-30 AWG, about 60 mm. Twist the LED pair (A, K) together and the detector pair (C, E) together, about one turn per centimetre.

Does the 60 mm pigtail beside the motor need anything?

The detector side is the sensitive one. Its collector node feeds the LM393 input through a pull-up of about 10 kΩ [E], which is a high-impedance node. A wire beside the motor can couple the motor's PWM edges (8 V in tens of ns) into it. 2 pF of coupling [E] at about 160 V/µs gives roughly 0.3 mA [E], a spike of volts on a 10 kΩ node for a fraction of a microsecond. The comparator has no hysteresis on most modules [E], so near its threshold that becomes extra edges. The run is short and mostly under the core, away from the motor leads, so the risk is modest. The fixes are cheap, so this design includes them:

  • Twist the detector pair (C, E) and the LED pair (A, K). Twisting cancels most of the coupled pick-up and costs nothing.
  • C5, 10 nF across the module's C and E pads [C]. With the 10 kΩ pull-up it is a 0.1 ms low-pass on the detector signal. At top speed a window lasts 9.4 ms, so the edges barely move. The TCRT5000 itself is slower than that filter anyway: 10 µs rise and fall, but much slower at the low light levels it sees [D Vishay]. Solder C5 on the module's underside, legs short.
  • No shielding is needed at these lengths [E]. If you still see stray counts with the robot still and the motor running (irw 1), first move the pigtail further from the motor leads. Then double C5 to 22 nF.

The LED pair carries a steady 10-20 mA and is not sensitive.

The alternative: a bare TCRT5000 and two resistors into GPIO34

You could drop the module entirely. Run the LED from 3V3 through a resistor (about 120 Ω, 17 mA [E]), give the phototransistor a pull-up (10-47 kΩ, picked by trial), and wire the collector straight to GPIO34. Fewer parts, no desoldering, and only one 4-wire cable.

I recommend keeping the module, for a beginner especially:

  • It sets its own threshold. The comparator gives clean digital edges at a threshold you set with the trimmer, and its D0 LED shows you when it switches. That makes the setup in "Adjusting the trimmer" something you can see.
  • The bare version has no threshold you can turn. It depends on the pull-up value, the ring's contrast, the gap and the room light. It is set by changing resistors.
  • Slow edges miscount. The bare collector voltage moves slowly as a window edge crosses the spot, over milliseconds at low wheel speed. GPIO34's input has no Schmitt trigger [E], so a slow edge can fire several interrupts more than 1 ms apart. The firmware's lockout would not catch them, and the count would be wrong at exactly the low speeds where balancing lives. Reading it on the ADC with hysteresis in software would fix that, but it is a firmware change, and the agreed firmware uses an edge interrupt.
  • It matches the published robot, so the same skills, parts and firmware carry into stage 2.

The bare version is worth it only if you have no module, or the module refuses to switch on your ring.

Design

  • Supply: 3.3 V, from the ESP32's only 3V3 pin. The D0 pull-up goes to the module's own VCC [E]; on 5 V it would put 5 V on GPIO34, which is a 3.3 V pin.
  • Sharing the 3V3 pin (the split). The IMU's W24 already sits on it. The split is a Y-lead (W28) made off the robot, in place of a joint on JB: JB has no 3.3 V, and a splice on the robot would mean soldering there. W28's Dupont female goes on the 3V3 pin. About 3 cm along, the wire splits: one branch ends in a single male header pin that W24's female plugs onto, the other runs to K3. The ground is split the same way (W29) on the row-A GND pin with W16. That keeps the whole sensor cable on row A, as the mechanical route expects. The IMU now reaches 3V3 through one more Dupont contact. A contact is good for an amp or more [E] and the IMU draws 5 mA, so the extra contact is a reliability matter, not a current one. Tie the Y-lead to the ESP32's tie so nothing pulls on it.
  • 3V3 budget. The module draws about 15-25 mA at 3.3 V [E]: the IR LED through its series resistor (10-20 mA [E]), the LM393 (0.4 mA [D TI LM393]) and its two indicator LEDs (1-2 mA each [E]). The DevKit's AMS1117 regulator is rated 800 mA [D]. With the ESP32 (no radio, 30-68 mA [D]) and the GY-521 (5 mA) it carries under 0.1 A and dissipates about (5.0 - 3.3) V x 0.1 A = 0.17 W [E]. The Mini360 sees about 25 mA more. At the pack it is about 10 mA [E].
  • Output stage. The LM393's output is open collector [D] with a pull-up of about 10 kΩ on the module [E]. A strong reflection (a window, showing the yellow rim) drives D0 low and lights the D0 LED [D listings]. A black bar lets it rise. With R5 the high level is 3.3 x 100 / (100 + 10) = 3.0 V, above the ESP32's 2.5 V logic-high threshold (0.75 x 3.3 V [D]). The low level is under 0.4 V [D LM393].
  • R5, 100 kΩ pull-down on GPIO34. GPIO34 has no internal pull resistors [D ESP32]. With the module unplugged it would float and pick up the motor's PWM as false edges. R5 holds it at 0 V, which the firmware reads as "no sensor". R5 is on the robot side of K3, so it stays when the module is unplugged.
  • C4, 10 nF on D0. The cable is tied with K1, right beside the motor leads. C4 with the module pull-up gives a 0.1 ms rise time constant. The fall is fast because the LM393 sinks it. Spikes are filtered and real edges barely move.
  • Edge rate against the firmware. The fastest the wheel turns is no load, about 200 rpm = 21 rad/s [E, the simulator's figure]. That is 3.3 turns/s x 32 = 107 edges/s, one every 9.4 ms. The simulator's largest balancing speed, 0.64 m/s [S], gives 100 edges/s. The firmware ignores edges closer than 1 ms (IR_LOCKOUT_US). That is a 9x margin, and it could count up to 1000 edges/s. The two 0.1 ms filters are about 1 % of the shortest edge spacing.
  • Chatter. With no comparator hysteresis, D0 can toggle a few times within microseconds at a window edge. The 1 ms lockout drops the repeats. If counts still double, turn the trimmer a little away from the switching point.
  • Light. Sunlight and incandescent light contain IR and can hold D0 one way. The clip shades the sensor. Check the switching with the room lights on.
  • Milestone A, no cable fitted. GPIO34 then floats. The firmware counts edges during the 1 s gyro calibration, when the robot is still. More than 4 edges means a floating input, and it stays on the IMU. If you plan milestone B, you can fit the cable (W28-W30 with R5 and C4) at milestone A: it holds GPIO34 low and changes nothing else.

Fitting it: no soldering on the robot

Do this after milestone A works, alongside the mechanical steps in mechanical.md (Milestone B, steps 1-6).

  1. Module and sensor, on the bench. Identify the pads and legs ("Which leg goes to which pad"). Take the sensor off, then solder the pigtail and C5.
  2. Sensor cable, on the bench. Make the two Y-leads (W28, W29). Crimp W28, W29 and W30 into the K3 socket in the order 3V3, GND, D0 (pins 1, 2, 3). Solder R5 and C4 across pins 3 and 2 behind the housing, and heat-shrink them. Make the module lead: three Dupont females for the module's VCC, GND and D0, crimped into the K3 plug in the same order.
  3. On the robot. Fit the sensor, ring, wheel and module as mechanical.md says. Unplug W24 (3V3) and W16 (GND) from the ESP32. Plug the Y-leads' females onto 3V3 (row A, 19th pin from USB) and GND (row A, 6th from USB), and plug W24 and W16 onto the Y-leads' male pins. Plug W30 onto IO34 (row A, 15th from USB). Tie the cable with K1 and plug K3.

Back to milestone A: unplug K3. R5 keeps IO34 low, and the firmware falls back to the IMU by itself.

Adjusting the trimmer

With the robot on and the wheels off the ground, turn the left wheel slowly by hand. The D0 LED must follow the ring: on over each window (yellow rim), off over each bar (black). If it stays one way, turn the blue trimmer slowly until it starts to follow. Find the trimmer positions where it stops following on each side, and set it midway between them. Check again with the room lights on.

Power-up (milestone B)

Do these after step 8 of the main checklist, with the robot otherwise working.

# Connect Do Expect
B0 Module with its sensor still on it, on the bench, powered from a 3.3 V supply (or the ESP32's 3V3 and GND on the bench) Hold the black ring material, then the wheel's yellow rim, 2-3 mm in front of the sensor. Power LED on. Yellow rim: D0 LED on, D0 under 0.4 V. Black: D0 LED off, D0 at 3.3 V (no R5 on the bench). If neither changes it, turn the trimmer. This proves the module before you take it apart.
B1 SW1 off. Sensor cable fitted, K3 not plugged. Ohms on the K3 socket, pin 3 to pin 2. Then SW1 on: volts on pins 1-2 and 3-2. About 100 kΩ (R5; C4 makes it climb for a moment). SW1 on: pins 1-2 = 3.30 ± 0.1 V; pins 3-2 = 0 V. show and balancing work as before: milestone A is unchanged.
B2 SW1 off. Sensor in its clip, module on the core, pigtail done. Meter on ohms across the module's A and K pads, then C and E (module unpowered). Check the pigtail. A-K: about 1.1-1.2 V in diode test one way, open the other. C-E: open in the dark. No pad shorted to another.
B3 Plug K3. SW1 on, wheels off the ground. Set the trimmer (above). Type irw 1 and turn the left wheel exactly one turn by hand. Power LED on. D0 LED on over each of the 16 windows. The edge count goes up by 32 a turn, with no double counts. D0: under 0.4 V over a window, about 3.0 V over a bar [E].
B4 Robot on the stand. motor 1 3000 with irw 1; then motor 0.3 1000 with the wheel held still by hand for a moment. About 100 edges/s at no-load speed [E]. No counts while the wheel is held still with the motor driving: a count then means noise (see the pigtail section). Pack current about 10 mA higher than in step 8 [E].

Troubleshooting

Symptom Likely cause Fix
0 V at BMS P+ / P- BMS waiting for a charger, or BM wire missing Plug the charger in for a second. Check the B-, BM, B+ order.
ESP32 resets when the motor starts 5 V from the wrong place, or the ESP32 ground only through a thin path W15/W16 must come from the Mini360. JB GND to MX1508 - must be W12, 22 AWG. Then add 100 µF across the ESP32's 5V and GND.
MPU-6050 not found A loose jumper, SDA and SCL swapped, or VCC on 5V Check W24-W27 against "IMU wiring". i2c_scan must show SDA=1 SCL=1.
Pitch goes negative when tilted forward GY-521 mounted differently from the drawing Remount X-up, chip forward, or change readImu().
Wheel twitches at switch-on R3 or R4 missing or not reaching the - pad Check IN1 and IN2 to - on ohms (about 100 kΩ each, ESP32 unplugged).
Motor weak or cutting out after hard work, one side of the MX1508 hot The weak MX1508 channel Move to channel B (see "MX1508").
vbat far from the meter Divider wrong, or W17 loose Measure VS: it must be 0.248 x pack.
Robot idles, LED blinking 1 Hz Low battery (6.4 V for 2 s) Charge. A reset clears it.
(B) No wheel counts while the wheel turns, D0 LED never changes Pigtail pair swapped, trimmer, sunlight, or K3 not plugged Steps B2-B3; check A, K, C, E against "Which leg goes to which pad".
(B) Counts while the wheel is still, or twice per edge Comparator chatter at a window edge, or noise on the pigtail or cable Turn the trimmer a little; check C5 and C4; twist the pigtail pairs; move them from the motor leads.
(B) D0 reads 5 V Module powered from 5 V VCC must come from 3V3 (W28).

Reference

What changed from the first-pass wiring

The first pass in ../README.md was right in its pins and its main power path. This design adds or changes:

Change Why
R3, R4: 100 kΩ pull-downs on MX1508 IN1 and IN2 [C] From reset until setup() runs (a few hundred ms) GPIO25 and GPIO26 are inputs with no pull [D ESP32 datasheet, IO_MUX reset state]. A floating IN pin can switch the bridge on for a moment and kick the wheel. The MX1508 may have internal pull-downs, but no datasheet available here says so for certain [E]. Two resistors make it certain: the motor stays in coast until the firmware drives the pins.
C3: 100 nF ceramic across the motor tabs [C] Brush noise suppression at the source, as Pololu recommends for brushed gearmotors [D Pololu]. It keeps commutator spikes off the long motor leads and away from the I2C wires and the ESP32.
JB, a small junction board on the mast front [C] The divider (R1, R2, C2) needs a home, and the battery rail needs one point where the MX1508 feed and the divider tap meet. JB carries both, plus the K2 power plug header. stage1.py gives it rails on the mast front.
K1 and K2, two JST-XH 2-pin connectors [C] K1, tied to the back of the core, lets the core (motor) come off the mast; K2 separates the battery and switch from everything they feed, so each step of the power-up can be checked before the next part is connected.
J1 charge jack and an 8.4 V charger [C] The first-pass list had no way to charge the pack in place. Same jack and charger as the published robot.
The Mini360 is fed from the MX1508 pads, not from a separate tap [C] Shortest wires on the back of the mast. The ESP32's ground then reaches the battery through the Mini360 and the MX1508's - pad, so no motor current flows through the ESP32.
IMU on 20 cm jumpers, not 10 cm [C] The ESP32's I2C pins are on the back of the mast, about 16 cm along the cable route from the GY-521 on the front of the core (mechanical.md). 10 cm jumpers do not reach.
MX1508 channel A only; IN3, IN4, MOTOR-B not connected Stated, so nobody wonders. See "MX1508" for the case where channel A turns out to be the weak one.
No firmware change Every pin and constant in the sketch matches this circuit; the generator checks it. Two optional firmware tweaks are listed at the end.
Firmware notes (no change made here)

The sketch matches this circuit: IN1/IN2 on GPIO25/26, SDA/SCL on 21/22, battery on GPIO36 through 100k over 33k, LED on GPIO2, MPU-6050 at 0x68, 20 kHz 10-bit slow-decay PWM, 6.0 V cap, 6.4 V low-battery stop. Two optional changes, for whoever owns the firmware:

  1. Make the bench motor command refuse to run while lowBatt is set (today it is checked before the low-battery branch), so it cannot drive the motor from USB power through the Mini360.
  2. If step 6 shows the battery reading off by more than 0.1 V, add a BATT_CAL factor as the published robot has.
  3. (B) The sketch now has the wheel sensor: PIN_IR = 34 (the generator checks it against this circuit), a 1 ms lockout, trust after 8 believable edges, and a floating-input check during gyro calibration. Both a steady low (R5, module unplugged) and a floating pin (milestone A, no cable) end up as "no sensor".
